flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
Oh my goodness. So many things come to mind. Let me see, which one should I use in particular? Time a student was having a really hard time. I had one student, it wasn't necessarily behavioral. They were just kind of having a hard time in their day. Their like grandparents had passed away and they it was like their first day back in class and they didn't know. They didn't really know how to process it yet or how to say anything. And they were sort of acting out of character, you know, brushing things off their desk, throwing things kind of just had an off day. But it was very out of character. So I was able to pull him out of the classroom and tell him at my school, you saw my training. So a lot of that language, I see you're doing this, you know, it looks like you're feeling upset. And that's sort of what we use at my school. So I used our summer training and. He felt comfortable enough. He actually started crying and was saying, Ms. Gonzalez, like, I'm so sorry, I know he's the second grader that, you know, I know I was throwing my stuff. I shouldn't do that. And then he was able to open up and tell me about his day. My most important thing, working with kids is definitely building that relationship first. So that when they do. Have a hard time or a difficult time, you already have that foundation and rapport with them. So.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or saying no. Walk me through exactly what you would do, step by step
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q5 Attempt 1]
Okay. For a three-year-old, when I have worked, I worked as an RBT, and that was typically the age range for the clients that we had was anywhere from two to five. So I have worked with the younger kids, and they were diagnosed with autism or they were nonverbal. So what I did in that situation, also because they can't tell you that, hey, I don't want you to change my diaper right now. I would just, in that situation, if they were not letting me change their diaper, maybe see if they're... I guess I'm just kind of like, is there a um, situation? Like, do they have a rash or, like, what is, what's going on with the child? Um, I would see if maybe there was a bigger issue, like I said before, like a rash or some reason why they wouldn't want it or, like, wouldn't want a diaper changed. Um, make sure that, um, they are, maybe not change them in that moment, but not wait, like, kind of, just get them to be, um, get them back to that baseline of being, um, calm and, um, kind of figure out what is going on with the baby, and then not change the diaper until we were back to that point.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time something didn’t go as planned at work and your role in it. How did you handle the responsibility piece?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q7 Attempt 1]
Um, there was a time when it was another teacher's lesson plan and, um, the way it was laid out, it just didn't, um, the kids weren't really understanding the point we were trying to get across. Um, I didn't have any of the materials that I needed for the lesson plan that they gave us. Um, and it kind of just put me in a position to learn how to improvise in the moment that, okay, I just need to make sure this is as beneficial of a lesson or activity for the kids as I can, even though I don't necessarily have everything I need for what was given, I'm going to figure it out and I'm going to make it the best lesson possible for the kids. So it definitely, um, helped me learn. How to improvise in the moment and be able to, um, like redirect, even if something isn't going exactly how it's supposed to. Um, it was in math and it was asking to use manipulatives in the classroom. And, um, we weren't given, um, my school just didn't have the manipulatives at the time. Um, and I was able to, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, um, to, um, kind of just pull things from the classroom and have the kids use those for manipulative. So they're still getting the hands-on aspect of the math.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time you had to work closely with another adult in a challenging situation. How did you navigate it?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q8 Attempt 1]
In my previous school year, me and I was in a TA position at the time, and my lead teacher and I didn't see eye to eye on how we should be running our classroom. I felt like the lead at the time was supposed to be in charge of the classroom, and then I was supposed to just do my TA duties and then behavioral management. But my lead would get mad at me or upset with me because I wouldn't be in the classroom because I would be redirecting the behavioral kids, and it sort of felt like this tension in the classroom between her and I because we were not on the same page. And so I asked her if we don't have to talk about it right now, but I would prefer if we talk about it before we go home today. Just so that when we come into the classroom tomorrow, we're able to be here for the kids and not because when you're off with your coworker, the kids can feel it and they can tell maybe something's going on if they don't know what it is. But I made sure we had that conversation and I didn't approach her in any type of accusatory way. I just said, I would love it if we could sit down and just have a conversation about. The expectations in the classroom and how.
